_note: Sites triaged as acceptable fail-open reads, each with a reason a reader can check against the source -- the same convention as tools/reachability_exemptions.json. Keyed on (file, var) rather than line: line numbers shift on every edit and a stale line silently un-accepts an entry. The cost is that two variables of the same name in one file are accepted together, so check that before adding one. An entry that matches nothing is reported as STALE by the checker rather than ignored -- the first entry ever written here was resolved within the hour and nothing would otherwise have said so.

The fallback only affects rowId, which is a best-effort handle for the later usage measurement -- a statistic, never a control.

ACCEPTED, with the consequence stated. The value feeds excludeCredentials, the WebAuthn list telling an authenticator not to enrol a passkey it already holds. A failed read means the list is empty, so a user could register a SECOND passkey on the same authenticator. That is a duplicate credential row, not an access grant: no new person gains entry, nothing is overwritten, and multiple passkeys per employee are a normal and wanted state anyway. Refusing registration because a read failed would be the worse trade.

ACCEPTED, and already deliberately handled. The file carries its own comment: a bare ternary made a failing read indistinguishable from an unpublished profile, so a console.error was added on !sr.ok. The value is the shop's optional contact block on a public order-tracking page; its absence degrades the page rather than asserting anything false, and the failure is now in the log where an operator can see it.

ACCEPTED, and the direction is why. findIcd10Match() does `if (!r.ok) return null` on a public NLM ICD-10 lookup. Surfaced 2026-09-04 the first time this tool's default walk included app HTML. Both consumers were read, not assumed. sairncode.html:6598 turns a null into `{source:'none'}` -- a VERIFICATION source, so an unreachable API reports the code as UNVERIFIED rather than verified: it under-claims, which is the safe direction for a coding tool. sairncode.html:11774 falls through to a web-search tier whose own prompt says 'never invent a plausible-sounding code number'. Neither consumer reads null as 'no such code exists'. The function's comment states the rule it is keeping -- 'never invents a code if the API returns nothing' -- and the code keeps it. NOT accepted as a general licence for `if (!r.ok) return null` in this file: this is one function whose two call sites were both checked.
